Born on this day in 1912, Alan Turing *38 is widely recognized for his achievements in the realm of computer sciences and his legacy in LGBTQ communities. He entered Princeton in 1936 following studies at King’s College, Cambridge, and just before the publication of his influential paper, “On Computable Numbers,” in which he envisioned abstract machines (now called Turing machines) that became the basis of modern computers. After earning his Ph.D. in mathematics from Princeton in 1938, Turing returned to England, where during WWII he was central to the successful effort to decode the German Enigma ciphers, a crucial development in the Allied victory. Turing, an openly gay man when homosexual acts were still criminal acts in the United Kingdom, was convicted of “gross indecency." In order to avoid prison, he had to agree to undergo a series of estrogen injections. He died two years later. In 2019, a portrait of Turing by artist Jordan Sokol of Jersey City, NJ was unveiled at Princeton, serving “as a visible expression of Princeton as the welcoming community we are today, even as we continue to strive to become ever more inclusive and diverse in the years ahead." The portrait is located in the Lewis Library atrium. “For those of us in the LGBTQ community, Turing is an enduring icon, and the growing appreciation of his life and his great contributions to the world are a cause for hope and celebration," provost Jennifer Rexford .

Excited to share insights from my journey at Chaac Ventures over the past 4 months, where I met with 100+ startup founders across diverse industries, from healthcare to fintech to AI. Here are some key learnings that might be helpful for young founders starting on their journey: 💡Know Your Investor: Not all startups are meant for venture capital. Some businesses thrive better with more traditional investors. Learn the difference and understand if your venture aligns with the expectations of VC returns. 🤝 Relationships First: One of the most common pitfalls I’ve observed is the rush to pitch when meeting with VC firms. Instead, take the time to foster a genuine connection. Start with an introductory conversation to understand each other’s visions and values. Building a relationship lays a solid foundation for future collaboration and ensures alignment between your goals and theirs. 📝 Effective Material: Sending materials ahead of meetings can be a game-changer, but it’s crucial to do it right. Keep it concise and impactful – opt for a sleek one-pager and a visually appealing deck rather than bombarding them with lengthy documents. Remember, respecting the team’s time is key. Make every word count! 🎯 Less is More: Founders often fall into the trap of overwhelming investors with extensive research. Remember, simplicity is key. Focus on conveying your core message clearly and succinctly. It’s not about how much you say but rather how effectively you communicate your value proposition. If you are launching, scaling, or looking to join an early-stage tech startup, I would love to connect! Reach out at yash@chaacventures.com . #StartupTips #VentureCapital #FounderAdvice #TechStartup

Samuel Wright II ‘22's average workday looks a bit like his days as an undergraduate defensive lineman with Princeton Football: workout, practice, film. Instead of preparing for 60 minutes on the gridiron, Wright serves on the pit crew for RFK Racing's No. 60 team, driven by Ryan Preece. As a jackman, he jumps over the wall with a 25-30lb jack to lift the nearly 3,400lb car in 9 seconds or less. An architecture grad from Lawrenceville, GA, Wright carries many of the lessons he learned at Princeton with him on pit row and beyond. "Princeton taught me that being in the right place doesn't always mean being in an easy place … Football taught me to keep showing up, keep doing my job, and keep being accountable to the people beside me regardless of what else was happening around me." Accountability is a major part of his role race day. "You have to perform in a matter of seconds, your mistakes are visible, there's constant 'noise' around you, and there are a lot of people depending on you. Princeton taught me how to operate under pressure without needing everything around me to feel comfortable or in order first." The pressure came on fast considering this career was never on his radar. While working at an architectural firm after graduation, he received a call from a NASCAR recruiter who had seen his football tape. The size and speed of the All-Ivy defensive lineman as well as ability to be a good teammate met the requirements of the job. "Team identity, team culture, team chemistry, they spread among all of us before that season. We had one heart, one mind, and we had the same goal in mind," said Wright of his time on the undefeated 2018 Ivy League championship Princeton Football team. Wright's love of reading has also been an asset to his performance. In fact, he wanted to be a librarian when he was a kid. In between pit stops, when the adrenaline rush is at a high, you can find Wright getting lost in a book. "That way when it's time to perform, I can rely on and trust my instincts that I developed in practice instead of overthinking a moment." Read a senior year football feature about Sam: https://bit.ly/4q5zXYS

A few years ago, I had to relearn how to speak. Today, I talk to enterprise customers in New York for a living. Growing up in South Africa, I always believed my future was in sport. I spent years training full-time with the national team, chasing that dream with everything I had. When I came to Princeton, I kept chasing it, training, racing, and coaching every waking moment of the day. Then, during my sophomore year, I was hit by a car while cycling. It derailed my entire life. I went through speech rehab and had to relearn how to walk, how to concentrate, how to think. The basics most people never have to think twice about. For a while, it looked like I might never row again. It took a full year to come back. When I finally did, we won the East Coast Championships, placed second at Nationals, and traveled to Henley Royal Regatta in the UK, where we placed second again. By graduation, I had three paths: go back to a national team environment, go to grad school, or do something completely uncharted. I chose Rilla . Honestly, I didn't even know what the company was. In one interview, someone was throwing a football around in the background. In another, people were shooting each other with Nerf guns. It wasn't until I got the offer that it hit me: oh wow, this is a real company. So I sat down and thought hard about the environment I wanted, the person I wanted to become, the skills I wanted to train. And the more I dug in, the more I realized how well I aligned with Rilla's culture: competitive, resourced, hundreds of people pulling toward the same goal, trusted to do what's right for the team. It reminded me of the locker room. I told myself, it's just a year. Who doesn't want a year in New York? What I found instead was fulfillment I wasn't expecting to find outside of a boat. The same competitive drive I only ever associated with rowing shows up for me here. I'm building toward a goal surrounded by people who push me. And I am still growing. Because at rilla, the learning never stops. I get to keep the parts of sport I loved most: the team, the culture, the singular focus, the autonomy to go after a goal and own how I get there. One year in, and I'm just getting started. Excited for what's next.

Three of the four Fields Medalists announced today by the International Mathematical Union are Princeton alumni: Yu Deng *15, John Pardon ’11, who is a former mathematics faculty member, and Jacob Tsimerman *11. The medal, awarded every four years to researchers under 40 years old, is one of the most prestigious awards in mathematics. Christopher Skinner, Princeton professor of mathematics and chair of the department, extended warm congratulations to all of the 2026 Fields Medalists. “The awarding of the Fields Medal every four years is an opportunity to celebrate some great mathematics," he said. "But it is especially thrilling for the department to have the remarkable works of three of its alums awarded medals this year,” Skinner said. "Yu Deng *15, Jacob Tsimerman *11 and John Pardon ’11 are exceptional talents, and we are delighted to see them getting this well-deserved recognition and to bask a little in the glow of their accomplishments."

Last month, I had the opportunity to participate in The Hastings Center’s Summer Undergraduate Bioethics Program. In early June, I joined 17 other undergraduates for five days of intensive discussions, debates, and lectures with scholars from the Hastings Center. We explored topics including disability ethics, sociogenomics, and the use of AI in aging populations. The program gave me a deeper appreciation for the interdisciplinarity and breadth of bioethics, while also serving as an introduction to key approaches and methods in the field. It was also a chance to learn alongside other students who have been thinking seriously about questions in bioethics. Thank you to Julia Kolak, PhD , Richa Venkatraman, and Ava Randel for facilitating the program, as well as to my fellow participants for all of the thought-provoking discussions. I’m excited to stay in touch and continue to explore bioethics in graduate school!
